did.abstract: The Norman Holmes Pearson papers consist of correspondence, writings, printed material, photographs, and audiovisual material that document a broad range of Pearson's professional and personal activities, including his research on Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ezra Pound, his management of the literary estates of H.D. and Bryher, and his activity as a professor of English and American Studies at Yale University. Documentation relating to Pearson's service in the Office of Strategic Services is partially redacted.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into nine series: I. Correspondence, 1839-1976. II. Editorial and Other Projects, circa 1880s-1975. III. Writings, 1829-1975. IV. Research Files, 1851-1978. V. Professional Papers, 1929-1983. VI. Photographs and Microfilm, circa 1909-1975. VII. Printed Materials, 1889-1975. VIII. Personal Papers, 1888-1975. IX. Realia, undated.

bioghist.head: Norman Holmes Pearson (1909-1975)
bioghist.p: Norman Holmes Pearson (Yale 1932), professor of English and American Studies at Yale University and officer in the Office of Strategic Services during the Second World War. Pearson collaborated with curator Donald Gallup to develop the Yale Collection of American Literature, playing an instrumental role in the acquisition of the papers of H.D. and Bryher.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: The Norman Holmes Pearson papers consist of correspondence, writings, academic and professional files, printed materials, photographs, and audiovisual materials that document a broad range of Pearson's professional and personal activities, including his research on Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ezra Pound, his management of the literary estates of H.D. and Bryher, and his activity as a professor of English and American Studies at Yale University. Documentation relating to Pearson's service in the Office of Strategic Services is partially redacted.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: In 1983, the Central Intelligence Agency claimed 14 documents from Pearson's papers and reviewed the documents in order to determine whether to declassify them. The CIA released three of these back to Yale in their entirety; they redacted or "sanitized" two documents; and they retained the remaining nine. At the time of processing in 2019-2021, flags marking the former locations of these documents had been disturbed from their original order; those flags that were found have been retained in a separate folder marked as such. A list of the titles of documents returned, redacted, and withheld appears in an appendix to this finding aid. For more information, consult the curator.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into three subseries: General Correspondence, Family Correspondence, and Third Party Correspondence. General Correspondence is arranged alphabetically by correspondent or heading and chronologically within files. Family Correspondence is subdivided for letters to and from Norman Holmes Pearson and third party letters. Third Party Correspondence is arranged alphabetically.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series I. Correspondence consists of personal, professional, family, and third party correspondence. Materials document Pearson's work as a university professor, including his role in the American Studies community in the United States and abroad, and development of Yale's literary manuscript holdings.

General Correpondence is largely professional in nature and includes both named files and subject-, project-, and event-oriented files. The latter, such as "American Studies," "Fulbright Scholarship," and "Doshisha seminar" have been preserved as found among Pearson's files or earlier processing of the collection. Folder headings are transcribed and in quotation marks.

Files can be found for college and university offices, departments, libraries, and presses, commercial publishers, booksellers, journals, and literary and cultural organizations. Correspondence with college and university offices often relates to lecture invitations. Correspondence with faculty of different departments often relates either to departmental searches for candidates or personal requests for recommendations, though sometimes concerns projects or books. Correspondence with libraries relates to research.

Named files for correspondence with individuals include writers, colleagues in literary and American studies, and former students, among others. Along with early curator of the Yale Collection of American Literature, Donald Gallup, Pearson played an important role in developing Yale's literary manuscript holdings; he had a hand, for example, in the acquisitions of the papers of H.D., Bryher, and Eugene O'Neill. He knew H.D., Bryher, and Ezra Pound, and communicated with others in their family and social circles, including H.D.'s daughter Perdita Schaffner, Richard Aldington, Islay, Kenneth Macpherson, and Robert McAlmon, as well as other domestic Imagists, including John Gould Fletcher. In some cases Pearson played a role in finding publishers for their work. He also served as executor for H.D. and Bryher.
Large files in the General Correspondence subseries include: Bryher, Horace Gregory, Sherri Martinelli, Ezra Pound, and William Carlos Williams.

Carbons of outgoing typescript letters from Pearson are common in this subseries. Pearson also sometimes wrote on the verso of letters to him, typically re-used academic documents or correspondence. One can also find manuscript notes in Pearson's hand in the correspondence folders.
Enclosures, such as third-party letters, writings, photographs, and financial records, can be found accompanying letters and are often described in folder notes. In cases where other materials were prevalent in correspondence files but could not be established as enclosures, such materials have been removed to a separate folder(s). For example, following several folders of correspondence with Robert Duncan, there is a folder for "Printed materials removed from Duncan, Robert." Folders of third party correspondence relating to a particular individual have also been preserved.
General correspondence collection materials chiefly in English, with some French, German, and Italian, and enclosures in Japanese and Hungarian.

In addition to the large run of General Correspondence documenting Pearson's personal and professional activities, there are letters to and from Pearson with members of the Bennett, Kittredge, Pearson, and other families. Of particular note is the rich and decades-long exchange between Pearson and his mother, Fanny H. (Kittredge) Pearson. Approximately 1,000 pieces of correspondence date from 1920 to 1963.

There is also a small quantity of third party correspondence consisting of contemporary material that likely came into Pearson's possession as enclosures, subsequently separated from accompanying correspondence, and older correspondence possibly acquired by Pearson for research or for the library.
Additional correspondence, including H.D.'s letters to Pearson, can be found among the mixed files for editorial and publishing projects in Series II. Editorial and Other Projects.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series II. Editorial and Other Projects pulls together textual projects on which Pearson served in an editorial or advisory capacity. Material relating to H.D. that was assembled by Pearson or by earlier processing of his papers can also be found here. These project materials are mixed in nature and can include correspondence, writings, and other papers, such as clippings, printed material, and financial and legal records.

Pearson contributed to numerous editorial projects during his academic career. Materials can be found in Series II for smaller, one-time projects and for larger undertakings, including the Oxford anthology of American literature (New York: Oxford University Pres, 1938), co-edited with William Rose Benét, and Poets of the English language (New York: Viking Press, 1950), co-edited with W. H. Auden, both of which were published in multiple editions.

Pearson's early academic work focused on 19th-century American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Before Pearson had even completed his graduate work, he edited The Complete novels and selected tales of Nathaniel Hawthorne (New York: The Modern Library, 1937), and later in his career, in the 1970s, he co-edited, with Thomas Woodson and L. Neal Smith, The Letters , volumes XV-XVIII of the centenary edition of the works of Hawthorne published by Ohio State University Press. The "Hawthorne Editions" materials in Series II are subdivided for correspondence and other papers and not differentiated by project title.

Pearson's relationship with the American poet H.D. is documented in a published selection of their correspondence, Between history & poetry (Iowa City: Iowa University Press, 1997). The H.D. (Hilda Doolittle) Material in Series II contains the original letters from H.D. to Pearson dating from 1937 to 1961, along with other correspondence, writings, and other papers. In addition to H.D.'s letters, for example, there are numerous correspondence files for publishers, booksellers, and libraries.

Other materials found in Series II relate to a Yale project, The Works of Jonathan Edwards (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1957-), Gandharan art in Pakistan (New York: Pantheon Books, 1957), by Islay Lyons, a member of H.D.'s social circle, and Decade: a collection of poems from the first ten years of the Wesleyan poetry program .
For royalty statements relating to editorial and other projects, see the subseries for Financial and Legal Records in Series VIII. Personal Papers.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series III. Writings contains work both by Norman Holmes Pearson and by others. The bulk of Pearson's writings consist of drafts and printed versions of shorter works, such as essays, lectures, forewords and introductions, and radio broadcasts and interviews. Writings date from student papers written while Pearson was an undergraduate at Yale University in the early 1930s to 1975, the year of his death, and document Pearson's research and teaching interests in American literature, culture, and history. There is also one copy (3 volumes), typescript carbon, corrected, of Pearson's dissertation The French and Italian notebooks by Nathaniel Hawthorne (1941).

Writings by others listed here in Series III are arranged alphabetically by author and then by title, with the exception of a group of "offprints" filed at the end of the alphabetical run. This group of writings likely aggregates material acquired by Pearson during the course of his own research, through work on editorial projects, and as solicited or unsolicited gifts from peers, students, and others. Printed versions (offprints and reprints) of essays are frequently inscribed to Pearson.

For additional lecture notes and drafts by Pearson, see the Lectures and Other Events subseries in Series IV. Research and Teaching Files. For writings by H.D., see the H.D. (Hilda Doolittle) Materials subseries in Series II. Editorial and Other Projects. Additional writings by others can be found scattered in the Subject Files subseries in Series IV. Research and Teaching Files. For printed versions of reviews, see Series VII. Printed Materials. See Series VIII. Personal Papers for Notebooks and Journals and School Papers.

arrangement.p: Organized into five subseries: Bibliographic and Card Files, Files Relating to Nathaniel Hawthorne, Subject Files, Lectures and Other Events, and Teaching Files.

processinfo.head: Processing Information
processinfo.p: Reprocessing of the Pearson papers in 2020-2021 revealed a lack of organization in the large group of Research files (formerly Series III), as well as some overlap between the Research files and Professional papers (formerly Series VI). In order to improve research use of these materials, the following updates were made: one, the teaching files previously arranged within Pearson's Professional papers (now Series V) were moved into Series IV. Research and Teaching Files; two, subseries were established in Series IV to consolidate and distinguish groups of material by format and subject matter, with files arranged alphabetically within each subseries; and three, in a small number of cases in which stand-alone writings or small groups of letters or other materials were found in a subject file, materials were removed to the appropriate series.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series IV. contains Pearson's research, teaching, and other academic files. There are subdivisions for card files consisting of bibliographic citations and research notes, materials relating to Nathaniel Hawthorne, subject files, lectures and other events, and teaching files. The card files consist of citations and notes made by Pearson on particular texts. The remaining files contain mixed material, including additional bibliographic citations, manuscript notes, writings, printed materials, correspondence, and photographs.

Pearson's early academic work focused on 19th-century American author Nathaniel Hawthorne. Before Pearson had even completed his graduate work, he edited The Complete novels and selected tales of Nathaniel Hawthorne (New York: The Modern Library, 1937). His Yale dissertation, The French and Italian notebooks by Nathaniel Hawthorne , was submitted in 1941. Later in his career, in the 1970s, he co-edited, with Thomas Woodson and L. Neal Smith, The Letters , volumes XV-XVIII of the centenary edition of the works of Hawthorne published by Ohio State University Press. The files found on Hawthorne here in Series IV relate to these different projects. In addition to transcriptions of Hawthorne's Italian diary and journals, for example, there are correspondence files, consisting of transcriptions and photostats, for Hawthorne, his wife Sophia (Peabody) Hawthorne, the children's governess, Ada Shepard, and his friend Horatio Bridge.

The subject files in Series IV contain mixed material by, about, or relating to various individuals and topics. In some cases, transcriptions of correspondence or writings, presumably made by or for Pearson in the course of his writing, instruction, and editorial activities, can be found among the subject files. Otherwise, the manuscript material in these files consists chiefly of autograph manuscript notes by Pearson and his typed notes and drafts. Drafts of lectures and course and instructional materials can also be found here. As in other parts of the collection, Pearson re-purposed course materials, and his autograph notes can be found on the verso of sheets for such courses as "English 57, American Literature, 25 February 1948" and "American Studies, Twentieth-century American Prose, 15 March 1950." Printed materials in these files include reprints and offprints of articles, booksellers' catalog description, clippings, and other ephemera. There are also photocopies of printed versions of writings by others.

Lectures and Other Events brings together materials relating to conferences, seminars, and other events attended by Pearson. Materials include notes and drafts for presentations made by Pearson at events outside his day-to-day teaching responsibilities. Teaching files, on the other hand, contains materials clearly associated with courses taught by Pearson. These files include reading lists, excerpts, exam questions, and manuscript notes.
Materials chiefly in English; some materials in French, German, Russian, Danish, and Greenlandic.

processinfo.head: Processing Information

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series V. aggregates Norman Holmes Pearson's professional papers that fall outside his editorial projects (Series II) and his academic research and teaching (Series IV). There are files for committees, associations, boards, and organizations on which he served, as well as events, such as conferences and tributes. The series features materials relating to Pearson's war-time service in the Office of Strategic Services (O.S.S.). Materials date largely circa 1942, when Pearson joined the O.S.S., to his death in 1975.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series VI. Photographs and Microfilm consists chiefly of photographic prints and microfilm, but there is also a small amount of cut film and several 35mm color slides. Photographic prints include sourvenir photographs, snapshots, and studio portraits organized into subdivisions for People, Places, and Other. There are photographs of Pearson, family members, friends, and colleagues dating throughout Pearson's life, circa 1909 to 1975. In addition to commercial packets of souvenir photographs of various locations in Europe, possibly acquired while Pearson was at Oxford or later, while working abroad during World War II, Pearson preserved photographs relating to professional and personal travel. Many of these latter photographs, arranged within the "Places" subdivision, includes images of Pearson, his wife Susan Silliman (Bennett) Pearson, and others.

There are photographs of William Rose Benét, Kay Boyle, Hermann Broch, H.D., Philip Larkin, Eugene O'Neill and Eugene O'Neill, Jr., and Ezra Pound. There are also copy photographs relating to the 1968 edition of Being geniuses together , a collaboration between Robert McAlmon and Kay Boyle, with Ernest Hemingway, McAlmon, Bryher, Philippe and Marie-Louise Soupault, Nina Hamnett, Eileen Lane, William Carlos Williams, Ethel Moorehead, Peggy Gugenheim, Clotilde Vail, and others.

The microfilm in the collection documents Pearson's research circa 1947 to 1961 and relates chiefly to Nathaniel Hawthorne. The bulk of the reels are reproductions of original manuscript material held at Yale and other repositories. The microfilm and any accompanying containers and paperwork have been retained to document Pearson's research interests and activity.
Additional photographs removed from a scrapbook ("Yale memory book") can be found in the subseries for Other Materials in Series VIII. Personal Papers.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series VII. Printed Materials consists of clippings, issues of periodicals, and other kinds of printed ephemera.

The loose clippings found here are arranged in chronological order. Periodicals brings together all stand-alone issues of journals, newsletters, and newspapers. The subject and travel files consist chiefly of printed materials, but some manuscript materials, such as completed financial records, can also be found. These subject and travel files have largely been preserved from earlier processing, though blank postcards, some likely acquired while travelling, have been aggregated by format and are arranged alphabetically by place in a separate subseries. Event programs have also been aggregated and further subdivided by type of event. The Other materials subseries includes all other forms of printed ephemera, such as book catalogs, business and calling cards, christmas cards, invitations, and pamphlets and brochures.
Chiefly in English; some materials in French, German, Italian, and Spanish.

arrangement.head: Arrangement
arrangement.p: Organized into six subseries: Appointment Books and Calendar Diaries; Family Papers; Financial and Legal Records; Notebooks, Journals, and Notes; School Papers; and Other Papers.

scopecontent.head: Scope and Contents
scopecontent.p: Series VIII. Personal Papers aggregates diverse materials not found in earlier series. Subdivisions for Series VIII. include Appointment Books and Calendar Diaries, Family Papers, Financial and Legal Records, Notebooks, School Papers, and Other Materials.

The first subdivsion includes appointment books and calendars for early and late periods in Pearson's life. There are diaries dating from 1918 to 1930 and 1969 to 1972 and appointment books from 1967 to 1975. Family papers consist of a small quantity of manuscript and printed materials relating to Pearson's wife, step-children, parents, and others. Financial and Legal Records are subdivided for Royalty Statements and Other Materials. Royalty Statements document earnings and other financials for editorial projects, the Oxford Anthology of American Literature and Poets of the English language , for contributions to the 1948 Rinehart & Company edition of Thoreau's Walden , and for publications of works by Bryher and H.D.. Other financial records include a large file of receipts documenting Pearson's book collecting and other expenses.

The subseries for Notebooks, Journals, and Notes includes both volumes and loose manuscript notes. Content includes what would appear to be course-related notes from Pearson's days as a student in the early 1930s as well as travel-oriented writings dating from as early as 1929 to 1971. School Papers feature various materials relating to Pearson's years as a high school student in Gardner, Massachusetts in the mid-late 1920s, a preparatory year at Phillips Academy in 1927-1928, and then undergraduate and graduate years at Yale and Oxford universities. In addition to some ephemeral and course-related materials, there are class notes and drafts of papers, some unidentified (as to date and institution). Other materials include address books, biographical information, drawings, passports, and other papers.
